title: Finding and rehearsing Eddie Cleanhead Vinson
summary: Cootie brought Vinson to New York, got him a proper horn and case, and coaxed him through his first rehearsal.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: So, I'm out there listening to the band at this roadhouse. They split up the band. I'm in the kitchen. And Cleanhair got up and started to singing. He wasn't singing with the band. He started to singing the blues. I come out of that kitchen and run right down front. I said,
"This is what I want."
(Laughter)
And that's how I found Cleanhead.
But he told me, or you told me, or somebody told me, that he couldn't take you seriously.
I'm telling you, he wasn't singing with the band. He was kidding and joking around.
With that falsetto and all that?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And that was what I wanted. And I heard him singing them blues. I -- and I told him I wanted him. I offered him this money, and I stuck with him.
Well, didn't you have a hard time? Because he had his dad there, in Houston, didn't he?
Yeah.
You had a hard time getting him away, didn't you?

No, not him. I eventually got him to New York. Eventually -- I had the band, all my band, picked. And I had called rehearsal. So I had to go down to the station to meet him. I had sent for him to come here. So he came in on the train. And he didn't have no case with his horn. Had this old silver horn under his arm. I said, "No, I can't take him into rehearsal like this, and this bald head." (Unintelligible.)
(Laughter)
So I had to stop him down at my manager's and get him a horn with a case.
No kidding.

Yeah. So, after I did that, we went on to rehearsal. So he was scared to death. And I didn't ask him to sing nothing. You know. He said, 'Oh, I want to go back home. I can't make it, and I done spent my money --'
(Laughter)

I had to bring him up to my house and talk to him. I said, 'You'll be okay, man, don't worry about anything.' 'Don't worry about a thing. Oh, you're going to make it. You're going to make it.' 'I can't compete with these boys. I can't do this.' I said, 'Yeah. You're going to make it. You're better than these boys.' So the next day, in rehearsal, I took him to the piano player. I said, 'What was them blues you was singing down there? You should sing those blues so they can get an arrangement on them.' So he said it was in the key of F or something. So I said, 'Start the blues in the key of F.' Said, 'Come on, sing the blues.' He got up and sang them blues, and everybody was all over him.
(Laughter)
Yeah.
Everybody was all over him. So I mean, he was happy then.
So then he was all right.
Yeah.
Isn't that funny?
But he was -- he couldn't read fast.
He couldn't read the music fast.
(Laughter)
Well, Cootie, then, he must have had a bit of difficulty, then, huh? To try to cut the music?
Yeah.
Did he -- did he work it out in the end?
Uh-huh.
He did.
Oh, yeah.
Well, did he actually speed up his -- the way that he got used to reading?
Yeah. He was scared.
Yeah.
He was scared. I stuck with him, you know.
Yeah.
Telling him, 'Everything's going to be okay.' 'Your reading's going to be okay.' 'Just go along,' I said. 'Everything's going to be okay.'
Well, I mean, he could solo, even then, couldn't he?
Oh, yeah.
I mean, they could hear that.
Oh, yeah.
